item.title: From Word via Email to AI Skills: Discussing the Evolution of Documentation and Why Neural Networks Need Business Context
item.description:
We've come a long way from sending requirements in Word via email to automatically generating documentation with neural networks directly from a developer's Merge Request. Often, this happens without analyst involvement until the final review stage. But does automation make our documentation better? In this article, I want to look back at the evolution of how we managed project documentation, discuss a non-obvious problem with AI that few consider, and show how to combat it. At the end, I'll share useful resources – a documentation repository example for two approaches (classic waterfall with Kanban elements and pure Scrum) with a ready-made AI skill for analyzing code changes. Learn about the evolution of working with documentation.

item.title: Human-centricity, or the quiet revolution in design
item.description:
One of the most significant changes in interface design in recent years is happening almost imperceptibly. The screen has ceased to be an independent product with a fixed information architecture. Now the user formulates a request, the agent performs the task and returns UI components along with text — a table, a graph, a card with an action, or a map. This approach is called Generative UI, or GenUI. But a reconfigurable screen by itself is not a revolution. The industry has been creating personalized feeds and adaptive layouts for a long time, but each time the user has to learn the system's language, just a different one. Two changes are now observed. The first is that the user's life situation, described in their own words, becomes the entry point into the scenario for the first time. The second is that the unit of work for a designer becomes a rule executed in millions of generated screens. Hence the term "human-centricity," which is so often heard alongside GenUI, and it should be interpreted literally. Read more

item.title: A Cap from Italy, Chinese Hieroglyphs in a Letter — How It All Led Us to AI
item.description:
SIBUR plans to increase exports, including to China, Vietnam, and Arab countries. What this means: more emails from foreign clients with product photos, PDF attachments, and long correspondence chains. Previously, people handled this: before passing the task to a specialist, they analyzed who was writing, what they wanted to produce, and what help they needed. Now, all this had to be deciphered in different languages as well. So, we decided to build an AI assistant: let it read correspondence and compile reports. But something went wrong. Read more

item.title: How We Stopped Manually Designing Tables and Entrusted Processes to AI
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Alexander Antipov, and I am the product owner of MWS Tables, a platform for collaborative work and automation based on tables. Previously, tables on the platform had to be assembled manually: adding columns, selecting field types, setting filters, etc. Now we have an AI assistant that creates tables from a simple text description. We've also taught it to link tables, write formulas, configure data display, and much more. Today, I'll show you how to apply these new capabilities in practice. Read more

item.title: What to Back Up in an AI Application: Model, Documents, Indexes, or Dialogue History?
item.description:
Hello, Habr! This is Mikhail Vitko, PaaS Product Manager at Reg.ru. Imagine this scenario. After recovery, an AI assistant accepts requests and responds without errors. But when asked about the return period for a product, it states 14 days instead of 30: the database already knows about the new regulation, but the search operates on the old index. A service availability check won't detect such a failure. This article will delve into how to back up a RAG assistant for corporate documents and restore its parts in a consistent state. The topic is extensive, so we've divided the material into two parts. In the first, we'll discuss what data needs to be saved, what can be recreated after a failure, and how to organize backups in S3, PostgreSQL, and Kubernetes. In the second, we'll cover how to restore the application without data inconsistency and verify its correct operation after a failure. Read on.

item.title: There Was Never Software for Oil Formulations — A Custom Neural Network Reduced Development from Six Months to One Month
item.description:
There's a job like this — for several years in a row, calculating ratings of Russian industrial companies based on open data. In the last year, I've been seeing the same type of case more and more often: a company's vendor is leaving, and there's simply no ready-made product to replace it. Gazprom Neft faced exactly this situation with oil formulations — there was absolutely no one to buy from, because such a product had never existed. I'm figuring out how the company built its "Alchemist" neural network and what this means for the rest of the industry. Find out the recipe

item.title: How to Build a Self-Hosted RAG System with a LangGraph Agent on Local LLMs
item.description:
Typically, RAG systems and AI agents are built around cloud APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) and managed vector databases. However, for many tasks, complete autonomy is crucial: resilience to sanctions and independence from external providers. In this article, I'll explain how I designed and built an analytical system that aggregated over 12,000 news items in two weeks: from collecting RSS feeds to a smart agent that calls tools itself. We'll cover the journey from architecture to the pitfalls I encountered. Stack: Python 3.12, FastAPI, PostgreSQL + pgvector, Celery, LangGraph, Ollama (Qwen 2.5 14B, BGE-M3), Streamlit, Langfuse, Docker. Read more

item.title: MITRE ATT&CK in Detective Guise: A New Format for Security Training
item.description:
A rule can be read, but a habit can only be trained. This is the idea behind "CyberDetective" – a browser game where Avito employees investigate attacks on a fictional company. The company is fictional, but the attack schemes are real: a forged executive's voice, an invoice from a domain with a slight misspelling, a barrage of MFA requests, a stranger at an unlocked laptop. My name is Ilya Nikiforov, and at Avito, I'm responsible for Security Awareness in the GRC team: I train employees, conduct educational phishing campaigns, and work on generative AI security. I'm not a developer and have never made games. I conceived and built "CyberDetective" myself in 74 days: AI agents handled the code, tests, and reviews, and a colleague helped turn the prototype into a company service. I'll share what we created, what real attacks the tasks are based on, how the work was divided between me and neural networks, and how it all works internally – for those interested in the code. And why I believe that today, someone outside of development can create a useful product in their field. Read more

item.title: Episode 1. The Transformer goes to Atari Frostbite
item.description:
How is our brain structured and what information processes occur in it? What goals does it pursue? What data model and algebra can be used to represent its work? Why are we prone to various cognitive biases? How can we use our brain to its full potential? And so on and so forth. My name is Mikhail Kocherov. The questions above do not leave me in peace. I want to understand how our brain works. And what does it mean to understand? Is knowledge about brain morphology or its development from conception to death considered understood or not? To each his own. For me, to understand means to be able to reproduce, even in a simplified form. To grasp the key mechanisms and know how to assemble a working system from them that reproduces the intellectual properties of the brain. Read more

item.title: I made a screen to monitor my LLM provider quotas
item.description:
I'll start by saying that until recently, my knowledge of circuit engineering was at the level of not understanding the difference between a transistor and a resistor. Of all the tools somewhat applicable to embedded, I only had Rust. But when the so-called embedded AI (machine learning and computer vision directly on cheap microcontrollers) appeared on the radar, my sporting interest took over. Without spending weeks on theory, I just drove to the radio market and returned with a gentleman's set for a pioneer: ESP32, the first screen I found, and an encoder. My ambitions to run neural networks immediately crashed against the harsh reality of the first evening: how to make this piece of textolite come alive and display at least a couple of digits on the screen? The digits were quite specific. I have several LLM subscriptions, and each has its own limits: a five-hour window, a weekly window, a monthly ceiling. They reset at different times, live on different sites, and you can only find out the remainder by opening the right tab. I wanted to lift my eyes from the keyboard and immediately see what else the quota would be enough for. As a result, I got a desktop monitor: a native application that doesn't consume much memory for Windows, which collects the limits of four subscriptions, and a small screen with ESP32 showing them right in front of my eyes. Read more

item.title: Clean Room: An Agentic Laundry for Your Dirty Legacy Code
item.description:
Two out of three API calls returned HTTP 500. Agents layered patches upon patches until the code became a tangled mess. Instead of another fix, I moved the system to a clean room, where an agent writes a new implementation without seeing the old one. This article details the migration mechanism, 15 rules to prevent new workarounds, and an experiment with 36 DeepSeek runs to see how agent behavior changes based on the code and rules it's shown. Enter the clean room.

item.title: vue-llm: AI SDK for Vue and Nuxt — streaming chat, Generative UI, and models directly in the browser
item.description:
If you've built an AI feature in Vue, you've likely encountered the same issue: most LLM interface tools are designed for React, requiring adaptation for Vue or manual implementation of streaming, tool calling, and chat state. I created vue-llm, an open-source library that addresses this for Vue 3, Nuxt, and even Vue 2.7. Here are the links to try it out: • Playground without an API key (model downloads and runs directly in the browser on WebGPU): https://vue-llm.js.org/ru/playground • Russian documentation: https://vue-llm.js.org/ru/ • GitHub: https://github.com/dadashi44/vue-llm • npm: npm i vue-llm Read on

item.title: Auto-editing in Claude — Scam or Real Revolution? AI Video Generation in Claude in Russia
item.description:
Did you know that Claude can now edit videos? Not just write a script or give suggestions, but do it all itself. You put the source material in a folder and write: 'Remove pauses, stutters, and filler words, keep the best takes, add subtitles.' A couple of minutes later, a finished video is in the same folder. The project that can do this has gathered over 30,000 stars on GitHub in six months, and social media claims Claude edits better than specialized AI video tools. We checked if this is true. It turns out Claude doesn't watch your video at all before editing. How does it produce such high-quality results? Read on to find out. Read more
